name: Tracking Growth
title: Tracking Growth
answer: Tracking growth means monitoring English learners' progress in both language proficiency and content learning, using tools like proficiency growth charts to see whether a student is advancing through English levels at a healthy pace. It matters because a stalled growth pattern can trigger a conversation with the English language development team, and because a tool's average effect can hide which students it actually helps most.

sections.body: Tracking growth is the practice of following an English learner's development in two dimensions at once, language proficiency and content knowledge, rather than looking at either alone. Proficiency growth charts make the pace of movement through English levels visible, so a teacher can see whether a student is progressing at a healthy rate or has plateaued. The problem it solves is that stalled growth can otherwise go unnoticed until it becomes a larger academic problem. By flagging students whose growth has stalled, the chart turns a quiet pattern into a concrete starting point for action. That flag is not an answer in itself, it begins a conversation with the English language development team.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom or school, a teacher can use Google Sheets to chart annual proficiency scores and mark the students whose growth has stalled. That flag then starts a conversation with the English language development team, who can decide what kind of support to add. The text gives one grade band example: a scaled literacy program redesigned for English learners in kindergarten through third grade produced mixed results overall, with the largest benefits going to second and third grade students who had weaker reading skills. This means teachers should look at results for their own students rather than relying on a tool's average effect. Growth data should also guide the fade of support, so a student whose English is growing quickly may be ready for less translation and simpler frames, while a student whose growth has stalled may need more targeted help rather than more of the same tool.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this idea's evidence through a study of a scaled literacy program redesigned for English learners in kindergarten through third grade, which found mixed results overall, with the largest benefits for students in second and third grade who had weaker reading skills (Connor et al., 2022). The finding is stated exactly that way in the book, and it carries a caution: a tool's average effect may hide which students it helps most. The text does not present additional studies or figures for the growth chart practice itself, so that part rests on the practical guidance given rather than on a separate research finding. Teachers are told to check results for their own students, which follows directly from the mixed and uneven results described.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits on what data can do. Growth data informs decisions, but teachers make them, so the judgment about fading support or adding targeted help stays with a person. A student whose English is growing quickly may be ready for less translation and simpler frames, while a student whose growth has stalled may need more targeted help, not just more of the same tool. The flag from a growth chart is not a verdict, it starts a conversation with the English language development team. Because a tool's average effect may hide which students it helps most, teachers should check results for their own students rather than assuming a program works the same way for everyone. Nothing here is legal advice, it describes practice.
